scoreNote: Strong-adequate (4.5): grants that contrasting views usually drive progress, then argues the word 'any' is too absolute; two developed examples with analysis, controlled prose at about 400 words on a memorable First and Second skeleton.

sentences.text: New ideas often appear when people who think differently are forced to talk to one another.
Some people argue that progress in any situation requires discussion among those who hold contrasting points of view.
I agree that such discussion usually drives progress, but I think the word any makes the statement too absolute.
First, in most situations, debate between different viewpoints clearly improves results.
When people challenge one another's ideas, weak arguments are exposed and better solutions emerge.
For example, scientific progress depends on researchers questioning and testing each other's claims.
This shows that disagreement, handled well, sharpens thinking rather than blocking it.
A group in which everyone agrees too easily often misses obvious mistakes.
Hearing opposing views also forces people to understand a problem more deeply.
In most fields, then, contrasting opinions are a powerful engine of progress.

sections.role: Body 2 — Why it is not always required

sentences.text: Second, however, the claim that progress always requires such discussion goes too far.
Some situations call for quick, united action rather than lengthy debate.
Consider an emergency, such as a fire or a flood, where arguing over viewpoints would only cost lives.
In moments like these, agreement and speed matter far more than a clash of opinions.
Endless discussion can also trap a group in conflict, by contrast preventing any decision at all.
Sometimes a single determined person achieves more than a divided committee ever could.
Progress, then, does not depend on debate in every single case.
In conclusion, discussion among people with contrasting views usually does drive progress.
But in urgent or simple situations, unity and action can matter more than debate.
The wisest course is to welcome differing views in most cases while knowing when the time for talk has passed.
